outcomes: Compose linear layers and nonlinear activations into a trainable neural network.
Explain how nn.Module registers submodules, parameters, and persistent buffers.
Choose between Sequential and a custom forward method based on the computation rather than style.
Save, restore, inspect, and optionally compile a module while preserving an eager correctness baseline.

sections.title: Turn a fitted function into a network
sections.summary: A neural network alternates learned affine transformations with nonlinear operations.
body: An nn.Linear layer computes an affine transformation and owns its weight and optional bias as parameters. Stacking only linear layers still collapses to one linear transformation, regardless of depth. Nonlinear activations let the composition represent curved and piecewise relationships.
Keep the input and output contracts visible. A batch of N examples with F features has shape N × F; a regression layer that predicts one value per example returns N × 1.

code.title: A small regression network
code.source:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(1, 16),
    nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(16, 1),
)

batch = torch.randn(8, 1)
prediction = model(batch)
assert prediction.shape == (8, 1)

points: Layer widths define feature counts, not batch size.
The final layer shape must agree with the target and loss.
Parameters begin from an initialization and are changed by an optimizer.
The activation changes expressiveness and gradient flow.

sections.title: Study activations through outputs and gradients
sections.summary: Tanh, ReLU, GELU, and SiLU make different tradeoffs; none is universally correct.
body: An activation's forward curve shows which values it suppresses or preserves. Its derivative shows where a parameter can receive a strong, weak, or zero learning signal. Saturation, output centering, smoothness, and computational cost can all matter.
Compare activations under the same seed, initialization, data order, optimizer, and parameter budget. A different final loss is meaningful only when the rest of the experiment is controlled.

code.title: Inspect activation gradients
code.source:
import torch
from torch import nn

x = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 201, requires_grad=True)
activations = {
    "tanh": nn.Tanh(),
    "relu": nn.ReLU(),
    "gelu": nn.GELU(),
    "silu": nn.SiLU(),
}

for name, activation in activations.items():
    x.grad = None
    activation(x).sum().backward()
    print(name, x.grad.min().item(), x.grad.max().item())

callouts.title: An activation is an experimental choice
callouts.body: Preserve Tanh where it clarifies the book's example, then compare current common alternatives without claiming that one wins every task.

sections.title: Use Sequential for a straight path
sections.summary: Sequential names and executes a simple chain while registering every child module.
body: nn.Sequential is appropriate when each module consumes the previous module's single output. It provides concise construction, a useful printed representation, and ordinary parameter registration. Ordered descriptive names can make checkpoint keys and debugging output easier to read.
Do not force branching, multiple inputs, residual additions, or conditional behavior into Sequential. Those computations are clearer in a custom forward method.

code.title: Name the stages of a sequential model
code.source:
from collections import OrderedDict
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(OrderedDict([
    ("hidden", nn.Linear(1, 16)),
    ("hidden_activation", nn.Tanh()),
    ("output", nn.Linear(16, 1)),
]))

for name, parameter in model.named_parameters():
    print(name, tuple(parameter.shape), parameter.numel())

sections.title: Subclass Module when the computation has structure
sections.summary: Assign state in __init__, express data flow in forward, and let __call__ manage module behavior.
body: A custom module must call super().__init__() before assigning submodules. Modules stored as attributes are registered recursively, so parameters appear in parameters(), follow device transfers, and enter state_dict(). Raw tensors that should be learned must be wrapped in nn.Parameter; non-learned state can be registered as a buffer.

Define forward() but invoke the module as model(inputs). Calling forward directly bypasses the machinery around hooks and module calls. The forward method can use normal Python and ordinary tensor operations.

code.title: A custom residual-style regressor
code.source:
import torch
from torch import nn

class Regressor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width: int = 16):
        super().__init__()
        self.input = nn.Linear(1, width)
        self.hidden = nn.Linear(width, width)
        self.output = nn.Linear(width, 1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        features = torch.tanh(self.input(x))
        features = features + torch.tanh(self.hidden(features))
        return self.output(features)

model = Regressor()
assert model(torch.randn(4, 1)).shape == (4, 1)

callouts.title: A plain list does not register children
callouts.body: When storing a variable collection of layers, use nn.ModuleList or another module container so parameters remain visible to the optimizer and state dictionary.

sections.title: Inspect and preserve module state
sections.summary: A state dictionary contains parameters and persistent buffers under stable hierarchical keys.
body: The optimizer receives model.parameters(), while diagnostics often benefit from named_parameters(). A state dictionary provides a flexible boundary for saving learned state without routinely pickling the entire Python model object.

Construct the intended architecture before loading. Use weights_only=True during deserialization and strict loading when the checkpoint is expected to match exactly. The restricted loader narrows what can be reconstructed, but a checkpoint from an untrusted source must still not be loaded. For best-model tracking in memory, copy the state because state_dict() values refer to live tensor state.

code.title: Round-trip a state dictionary
code.source:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import torch
from torch import nn

class Regressor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width: int = 16):
        super().__init__()
        self.input = nn.Linear(1, width)
        self.hidden = nn.Linear(width, width)
        self.output = nn.Linear(width, 1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        features = torch.tanh(self.input(x))
        features = features + torch.tanh(self.hidden(features))
        return self.output(features)

model = Regressor().eval()
with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    checkpoint = Path(directory) / "regressor.pt"
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), checkpoint)
    state = torch.load(checkpoint, map_location="cpu", weights_only=True)

restored = Regressor().eval()
restored.load_state_dict(state, strict=True)
example = torch.randn(3, 1)
with torch.inference_mode():
    torch.testing.assert_close(model(example), restored(example))

callouts.title: Restricted loading is not a trust boundary
callouts.body: weights_only=True limits the objects the unpickler may reconstruct, but PyTorch still warns never to load data from an untrusted source. Obtain checkpoints from a trusted origin and verify their integrity.

sections.title: Keep outputs compatible and optimize last
sections.summary: Loss functions define output expectations; compilation is a performance experiment after correctness.
body: A regression model may emit unrestricted floating-point predictions for MSELoss. A multiclass model used with CrossEntropyLoss should emit raw logits rather than applying Softmax or LogSoftmax in its final layer. Convert logits to probabilities only in an evaluation or reporting step.

PyTorch 2.13 can compile a callable or module to optimize supported workloads. Backend, Python-version, and compiler-toolchain availability vary by platform. Compare compiled and eager results on representative inputs, allow for warm-up, and benchmark on the target device. Keep eager mode available for debugging graph breaks and correctness.

code.title: Check before optional compilation

callouts.title: Compile is not a model redesign
callouts.body: Compilation should preserve the model contract. A speed claim requires representative timing; equal outputs alone do not prove a speedup. The default backend may also require a platform compiler toolchain.

modern.book: The chapter compares Sequential, ordered names, and a custom nn.Module.
modern.current: Retain the comparison and make registration rules explicit
modern.reason: Current Module behavior still centers on registered submodules, parameters, and buffers; understanding registration prevents invisible state and optimizer omissions.

modern.book: The model's parameter state is inspected as part of the learning process.
modern.current: Save state_dict() and deserialize with weights_only=True
modern.reason: State dictionaries are inspectable and less coupled to Python class pickling, provided the reconstructed architecture and state keys still match.

modern.book: Eager Module execution is the standard path.
modern.current: Offer torch.compile as an optional, tested benchmark
modern.reason: PyTorch 2.13 can optimize a supported module, but eager correctness and target-hardware measurements remain prerequisites.
